why: Each operation ships one product or a pair from different locations, so the question is how many pairs you can form. With n products and the most common location appearing f times, the answer is max(f, ceil(n/2)): either the big location forces f operations, or everything pairs up.
hints: Every operation ships at most two products. What is the lower bound from that alone? What stops you from always reaching it?

Products from the same location can never share an operation, so the most frequent location (count f) needs f separate operations. If f <= n - f, you can always pair to get ceil(n/2); otherwise the f copies dominate.
Count locations with a hash map, take f = max count, return max(f, (n + 1) // 2). O(n).
pitfalls: The order note ("products come together keeping the order") is a distraction; any two products can be picked.
Odd n with no dominant location needs one single shipment: ceil(n/2), not n/2.
Do not simulate pairing greedily from the front; [1, 3, 1, 2] would mislead an adjacent-pairs approach.
